title: The 5 Tallest Mountains in the Solar System, Ranked (Everest Isn't Top 10)

scenes.text: The solar system's five tallest mountains. Everest isn't top ten. Number two isn't on a planet.

scenes.label: Ascraeus Mons · ~15 km
scenes.text: Number five: Ascraeus Mons, on Mars. About fifteen kilometres from base to peak, the tallest of the three Tharsis volcanoes.

scenes.label: Boosaule Montes · ~18 km
scenes.text: Number four: Boosaule Montes, on Jupiter's moon Io. About eighteen kilometres, with a fifteen-kilometre cliff on one flank.

scenes.label: Iapetus ridge · ~20 km
scenes.text: Number three: the equatorial ridge of Iapetus, Saturn's moon. Peaks around twenty kilometres high, along 1,300 kilometres.

scenes.label: Rheasilvia peak · ~22 km
scenes.text: Number two: the central peak of Rheasilvia crater on Vesta, an asteroid 525 kilometres wide. Around twenty-two kilometres high.

scenes.label: Olympus Mons · 22-26 km
scenes.text: Number one: Olympus Mons on Mars. Twenty-two to twenty-six kilometres, depending where you call the base. Everest, base to peak, is under five.

description:
The five tallest mountains in the solar system, ranked by height from base to peak: Olympus Mons on Mars (about 22 to 26 km), the central peak of Rheasilvia crater on the asteroid Vesta (around 22 km), the equatorial ridge of Saturn's moon Iapetus (about 20 km), Boösaule Montes on Jupiter's moon Io (about 18 km) and Ascraeus Mons on Mars (about 15 km).
Measurements of the base are uncertain, so Olympus Mons and Rheasilvia are close to a tie. Everest rises under 5 km from its base; Mauna Kea about 10 km.
Would you climb a mountain three times Everest's height?
subject: Olympus Mons Mars
first_comment: Olympus Mons or Vesta's peak at number one? And what should we rank next?
ranking_by: height from base to peak in kilometres
